name: Bioluminescent Eye Modification
description: Introduces bioluminescent protein expression into the iris and optionally the sclera, causing the eyes to produce their own visible light. The glow is soft — enough to be visible in dim conditions, not enough to illuminate a room. Combined with prismatic iris resequencing, the effect is striking: eyes that glow gold, green, blue, or red in low light, dimming in bright conditions and brightening in darkness. The luminescence is independent of the tapetum lucidum modification — glow eyes produce light rather than reflecting it. Helix Biosystems' premium version allows voluntary brightness control, including full suppression. Street versions glow constantly, which makes sleeping with your eyes slightly open a noticeable problem. In the Shelf, glow eyes are the second most common eye modification after iris color change. They serve as both fashion and practical low-light identification — you can recognize a friend by the color and pattern of their eye-glow across a dark room.
source_organism: Photinus pyralis (common eastern firefly), Aequorea victoria (crystal jellyfish)
reversibility: Fully reversible with luminescent protein suppression
side_effects: Constant-glow versions illuminate the inside of closed eyelids, disrupting sleep
Eye-glow is visible on surveillance cameras — identifiable at distance
Bright-glow variants cause mild eye strain over time
Rare: luminescent protein migration to surrounding skin, causing facial glow patches
social_perception: Common and attractive. Glow eyes are fashion-forward without being radical. Popular in nightlife, performance, and social settings. Constant-glow users are sometimes avoided in movie theaters and sleep-share spaces.
story_hooks: A surveillance analyst develops a database of eye-glow signatures that can identify individuals at ranges far beyond facial recognition — glow eyes have accidentally created a new biometric
A glow-eye user's luminescence begins flickering in a regular pattern — analysis reveals it matches a data transmission protocol, and someone is using their eyes as a broadcast antenna
